stem: A 58-year-old woman who smokes has had 5 weeks of weakness climbing stairs and lifting dishes into high cupboards, with a dry mouth. Her strength improves after a few seconds of repeated effort. Eye movements are normal, sensation is intact, and knee reflexes are reduced.
oneliner: 58F smoker + 5 wk proximal weakness + dry mouth + strength improves with repeated effort + eyes normal + reduced reflexes → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her weakness?

options.A: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
options.B: Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors on muscle

whyNot.B: **Myasthenia gravis**: weakness gets **worse** with use, eyelids and eyes first
whyNot.C: **Botulism**: descending paralysis with cranial nerves and fixed pupils, no warm-up
whyNot.D: **Guillain-Barré**: ascending weakness with absent reflexes, no improvement with effort
whyNot.E: **Upper motor neuron**: brisk reflexes and spasticity

answer: Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels (Lambert-Eaton)
why: **Proximal weakness that improves with repeated use + dry mouth + low reflexes in a smoker** = Lambert-Eaton (often with **small cell lung cancer**). Antibodies block **presynaptic calcium channels**, so less acetylcholine is released; repeated firing builds calcium up and strength improves.
chain: Weakness that improves with repeated use

idea.rule: Presynaptic problem (LEMS) = better with use; postsynaptic receptor problem (myasthenia) = worse with use.
also: Botulinum toxin also cuts release (SNARE proteins)
Dry mouth = autonomic synapses use the same calcium channels

stem: A 76-year-old woman dies after 7 years of steadily worsening memory loss and confusion. At autopsy the gyri are thin and the sulci wide, the lateral ventricles are enlarged, and microscopy shows many neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the cortex. There was no history of gait trouble or urinary incontinence.
oneliner: 76F + 7 y progressive dementia + thin gyri, wide sulci + big ventricles + plaques and tangles + no gait or bladder problem → why big ventricles?
ask: What is the most likely cause of the enlarged ventricles?

options.A: Blocked CSF flow inside the ventricles
options.B: Poor CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
options.D: Loss of brain tissue, with CSF filling the space (hydrocephalus ex vacuo)
options.E: Overproduction of CSF by a choroid plexus tumor

whyNot.A: **Noncommunicating hydrocephalus**: headache, raised pressure, ventricles big upstream of a block
whyNot.B: **Communicating hydrocephalus** (after meningitis or bleeding): raised pressure, not shrunken gyri
whyNot.C: **NPH**: wet, wobbly, wacky; she had **no gait or bladder trouble**
whyNot.E: **Choroid plexus papilloma**, usually in children; no mass here

why: **Plaques and tangles + thin gyri and wide sulci** = Alzheimer **atrophy**. Lost brain tissue leaves space that **CSF passively fills**, so the ventricles look big while the pressure is normal.

idea.rule: Big ventricles + shrunken brain + normal pressure = ex vacuo; big ventricles + raised pressure = true hydrocephalus.
also: Also seen in Huntington (caudate atrophy) and advanced HIV dementia

stem: A 67-year-old woman with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension suddenly develops weakness of the right face, arm, and leg that is equally severe in all three. She has no sensory loss, visual field defect, or language trouble, and has a right Babinski sign. CT shows no blood, and MRI shows a 1-cm diffusion-restricting lesion deep in the left hemisphere.
oneliner: 67F + 20 y hypertension + sudden right face, arm, leg weakness equal in all + no sensory, visual, language deficit + Babinski + CT no blood + 1-cm deep DWI lesion → vessel pathology?
ask: Which vessel change most likely caused this?

options.A: Cardiac embolus to a cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery
options.B: Thrombus on a carotid atheromatous plaque
options.C: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of small penetrating arteries
options.E: Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus

whyNot.A: Gives a **cortical syndrome** (aphasia, neglect, field loss)
whyNot.B: Gives **cortical or border-zone** deficits and often amaurosis fugax
whyNot.D: **Subarachnoid hemorrhage**: thunderclap headache; CT shows no blood
whyNot.E: **Venous infarct**: headache, seizures, hemorrhagic lesion, not a deep lacune

answer: Lipohyalinosis causing a lacunar infarct in the internal capsule
why: **Chronic hypertension** thickens and hyalinizes the **small penetrating arteries** (lenticulostriates). Occlusion causes a **small deep infarct**; in the **internal capsule** it gives **pure motor hemiparesis** of face, arm, and leg with **no cortical signs**.
chain: Small deep infarct in internal capsule

idea.rule: Pure motor or pure sensory stroke without cortical signs in a hypertensive patient is a lacunar infarct.
also: Lacunes can also affect basal ganglia, thalamus, pons
Ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria-clumsy hand are other lacunar syndromes
Diabetes also causes small-vessel disease

stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes and a long smoking history suddenly lost vision in his left eye 1 hour ago, with no pain. The left pupil reacts poorly to direct light but normally when the right eye is lit. A fundus photograph of the left eye is shown.
oneliner: 68M + vasculopath + sudden painless monocular vision loss + afferent pupillary defect + fundus photo shown → why did he lose vision?
ask: Which of the following best explains his vision loss?

options.A: Occlusion of the central retinal vein
options.B: Separation of the retina from the pigment epithelium
options.D: Occlusion of the central retinal artery

whyNot.A: **Vein occlusion** shows diffuse hemorrhages (blood and thunder), not a pale retina
whyNot.B: **Detachment**: flashes, floaters and a **curtain** over vision
whyNot.C: **Optic neuritis** is painful on eye movement, in younger patients, with a normal fundus
whyNot.E: **Vitreous hemorrhage** gives floaters and a red haze, usually in proliferative diabetic retinopathy

answer: Embolus blocks the central retinal artery
why: An **embolus** (often from a carotid plaque) blocks the **central retinal artery**. The inner retina loses its blood supply and turns pale around a **cherry-red macula**, causing **sudden painless vision loss** and an **afferent pupillary defect**.

idea.rule: Pale retina with a cherry-red spot means arterial occlusion; a hemorrhagic retina means vein occlusion.
also: CRAO is an ophthalmic emergency: look for a carotid or cardiac source
Giant cell arteritis can occlude the central retinal artery (check ESR)
Amaurosis fugax is a transient version

image.prompt: Fundus photograph of the left eye: diffusely pale, milky-white retina with a bright cherry-red spot at the macula and narrowed retinal arterioles; optic disc slightly pale. No text or labels.

stem: A 31-year-old man who injects a homemade synthetic opioid wakes up one morning almost unable to move. Over several days he develops marked rigidity, a slow shuffling gait and a pill-rolling tremor. Several other users from the same batch have a similar picture.
oneliner: 31M + IV drug user, homemade synthetic opioid + rigidity, bradykinesia, pill-rolling tremor + others from same batch → which neurons died?
ask: Which of the following neuron populations was most likely selectively destroyed?

options.A: Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis
options.C: Serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei
options.D: Noradrenergic neurons of the locus ceruleus
options.E: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta

whyNot.C: Loss is linked to **depression and sleep** changes
whyNot.D: Loss is linked to **depression and early Parkinson** features, not acute parkinsonism

answer: MPTP is converted to MPP+, which kills nigral dopaminergic neurons
why: A contaminated meperidine analog contains **MPTP**, which **MAO-B converts to MPP+**. MPP+ enters dopaminergic neurons, **inhibits complex I** and kills them, so **nigrostriatal dopamine falls** and parkinsonism results.
chain: Complex I inhibited in dopaminergic neurons

idea.rule: Selective loss of nigral dopaminergic neurons causes parkinsonism, even in the young.
also: Other causes: neuroleptics, carbon monoxide, manganese
Idiopathic Parkinson: alpha-synuclein (Lewy bodies)
Rotenone and paraquat are linked to complex I toxicity

stem: A 3-day-old boy born at 33 weeks' gestation became jaundiced within hours of birth. He was pale, had an enlarged liver and spleen, and a positive direct Coombs test. He developed poor feeding, seizures and arching of the back, and died. The brain at autopsy is shown.
oneliner: 3d boy + preterm + jaundice within hours + anemia + positive Coombs + seizures, opisthotonus + brain at autopsy shown → why the brain damage?
ask: Which of the following best explains the brain findings?

options.A: Unconjugated bilirubin crossed the immature blood-brain barrier
options.B: Deposition of conjugated bilirubin from biliary atresia
options.E: Germinal matrix hemorrhage into the ventricles

whyNot.B: **Conjugated** bilirubin is water-soluble and **does not cross** the BBB; atresia causes pale stools later
whyNot.C: Gives **cortical or periventricular** injury, not yellow basal ganglia
whyNot.D: Causes purulent exudate over the surface, not **yellow nuclei**
whyNot.E: **Intraventricular hemorrhage** of prematurity puts blood in the ventricles, not **yellow-stained nuclei**

answer: Fat-soluble unconjugated bilirubin enters the immature brain
why: **Hemolytic disease** (Rh or ABO incompatibility) overloads the newborn with **unconjugated bilirubin**. It is **lipid-soluble** and crosses the **immature blood-brain barrier**, staining and injuring the **basal ganglia** (kernicterus).
chain: Basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei damaged

idea.rule: Only unconjugated bilirubin causes kernicterus, because it is lipid-soluble and unbound bilirubin crosses the BBB.
also: Prevent with phototherapy, exchange transfusion, anti-D (RhoGAM)
Risk is higher when albumin binding is displaced (sulfonamides)
Crigler-Najjar can also cause kernicterus

image.prompt: Coronal section of a newborn brain at autopsy: bright yellow staining of the basal ganglia and thalamic nuclei, with otherwise pale cerebral tissue. No text or labels.

stem: A 34-year-old glassblower burned his hand without noticing. Exam shows loss of pain and temperature sensation over both arms and shoulders in a cape distribution, normal vibration and position sense, wasting of the small hand muscles, and normal leg strength. MRI shows a fluid-filled cavity in the center of the cervical cord.
oneliner: 34M + burns without pain + cape-like loss of pain and temperature in both arms + normal vibration and position + wasted hand muscles + normal legs + central cervical cord cavity → which structure explains the sensory loss?
ask: Damage to which structure best explains the sensory loss?

options.B: Crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure

whyNot.C: Would give **leg weakness and upper motor neuron signs**; legs are normal
whyNot.D: Would cause **contralateral loss below the lesion**, not a bilateral cape
whyNot.E: Would affect **all modalities**, including touch and position

answer: Syringomyelia: a central cavity cuts the crossing pain and temperature fibers
why: The second-order neurons for **pain and temperature cross in the anterior white commissure**, right at the center of the cord. A **central syrinx** cuts them, producing **bilateral cape-like loss** while **dorsal columns are spared** (dissociated sensory loss). Spread to the **ventral horns** causes **hand atrophy**.
chain: Central syrinx in the cervical cord

idea.rule: A central cord lesion gives bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch and position.
also: Associated with Chiari I malformation
Late: corticospinal signs, Horner syndrome
Loss of pain leads to painless burns and Charcot joints

stem: A 68-year-old man has a sudden severe headache behind his right eye. Examination shows right ptosis, the right eye resting down and out, and a dilated, poorly reactive right pupil. Visual acuity is normal and the left eye is normal.
oneliner: 68M + sudden headache behind right eye + ptosis + eye down and out + dilated poorly reactive pupil + normal acuity → mechanism of the pupil?
ask: Which of the following best explains the pupil finding?

options.A: Compression of superficial parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve

whyNot.B: Gives a **small** pupil (miosis) with ptosis, as in **Horner**
whyNot.C: Gives **vertical diplopia** and a head tilt; the **pupil is normal**
whyNot.D: Angle closure raises eye pressure but does **not cause ptosis or a down-and-out eye**
whyNot.E: Would cause **loss of acuity** and an afferent defect, which he does not have

answer: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery compresses CN III, including its superficial parasympathetic fibers
why: A **posterior communicating artery aneurysm** compresses the **oculomotor nerve**, whose **parasympathetic fibers lie superficially**. They are lost first, giving a **blown pupil**, along with **ptosis and a down-and-out eye** from loss of motor branches.
chain: Loss of parasympathetic (pupil) and motor supply
Mydriasis, ptosis, down and out eye

idea.rule: Compression of CN III hits the superficial pupil fibers first; ischemia hits the core motor fibers and spares the pupil.
also: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm: blown pupil with ptosis
Uncal herniation: ipsilateral blown pupil
Diabetic microvascular CN III palsy: pupil spared

stem: A 64-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history has had 3 months of difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs, with a dry mouth. Knee reflexes are reduced. A chest CT shows a hilar mass, and serum antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels are found. When he squeezes the examiner's hand hard for 10 seconds, his grip becomes stronger and his reflexes briefly return.
oneliner: 64M + smoker + proximal weakness, dry mouth, low reflexes + hilar mass + antibodies to presynaptic Ca channels + grip strengthens and reflexes return after 10 s of effort → why the brief improvement?
ask: Which of the following best explains why his strength improves with sustained effort?

options.A: Upregulation of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors during exercise
options.B: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
options.C: Calcium accumulating in the nerve terminal with rapid repeated firing
options.D: Calcium release from the muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum

whyNot.A: Receptor number does **not change within seconds**, and his defect is **presynaptic**
whyNot.B: Nothing here **inhibits the enzyme**; that is how edrophonium or pyridostigmine act
whyNot.D: Muscle SR calcium sets contraction **after** the end-plate fires; his problem is **too little ACh released**
whyNot.E: Desensitisation follows **too much ACh**; he releases too little

answer: Residual calcium builds up in the presynaptic terminal during high-frequency firing (facilitation)
why: With fewer working **presynaptic Ca channels**, each impulse lets in too little calcium to release enough ACh. During **rapid repeated firing**, calcium enters faster than it is cleared, so **residual calcium accumulates** and each impulse releases more ACh. Strength and reflexes **briefly recover**.
chain: Too little Ca enters per impulse
Little ACh released: weakness, low reflexes
Rapid repeated firing: Ca builds up in the terminal
More ACh released: brief recovery of strength and reflexes

idea.rule: A presynaptic release defect improves with rapid repeated stimulation; a postsynaptic receptor defect worsens.
also: EMG: incremental response at high-frequency stimulation
3,4-diaminopyridine blocks K channels, prolongs depolarisation and lets more Ca in
Botulism also shows an incremental response (presynaptic)
Myasthenia gravis: decremental response, fatigue with use

stem: A 39-year-old man with type 1 diabetes for 22 years has burning pain in both feet, worse at night, and even bed sheets are painful. HbA1c is 9.8%. Pinprick sensation is reduced in a stocking pattern, but vibration sense and ankle reflexes are normal. Vitamin B12 is normal and nerve conduction studies are normal.
oneliner: 39M + type 1 DM 22 y + HbA1c 9.8 + burning feet worse at night + bed sheets painful + stocking pinprick loss + normal vibration, reflexes, B12 and conduction → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his pain?

options.A: Loss of large myelinated fiber conduction
options.B: Spontaneous firing of damaged small nociceptor fibers through sodium channel activity
options.C: Degeneration of dorsal columns from B12 lack
options.E: Infarction of a single nerve trunk

whyNot.A: This gives **numbness and lost vibration and reflexes**; his are normal
whyNot.C: **B12 is normal**, and dorsal column loss removes vibration sense
whyNot.D: Unilateral, in one distribution; his symptoms are **symmetric and stocking-shaped**
whyNot.E: **Mononeuropathy**: sudden, one nerve; not symmetric burning

answer: Hyperglycemic injury of small fibers causing ectopic nociceptor firing and persistent sodium channel activity
why: Chronic **hyperglycemia** injures **small unmyelinated and thinly myelinated fibers** (polyol and AGE damage). The damaged nociceptors **fire spontaneously** through **persistent sodium channel activity**, causing **burning pain** with normal conduction studies, which test large fibers.
chain: Burning pain, normal vibration and reflexes

idea.rule: Small fiber neuropathy = pain and temperature affected, vibration and reflexes spared.
also: Early diabetic neuropathy, alcohol, HIV and Fabry disease hit small fibers first
Confirmed by skin biopsy (low intraepidermal nerve fiber density)
Nerve conduction studies test large fibers, so they stay normal

stem: A researcher blocks synthesis of dynein in cultured sensory neurons. Kinesin levels are unchanged.
oneliner: Experiment: dynein synthesis blocked in neurons, kinesin unchanged -> which process fails?
ask: Which neuronal process is most directly impaired?

whyNot.E: Done by **membrane transporters**, not microtubule motors

why: **Dynein** is the **minus-end-directed** microtubule motor and moves cargo **from terminal to cell body**. Blocking it impairs retrograde transport.
chain: Cargo returns to the cell body

idea.rule: Kinesin = anterograde (plus end); dynein = retrograde (minus end).
also: Rabies virus, tetanus toxin and herpes use retrograde transport
Nerve growth factor signals return retrogradely
Axonal transport defects occur in some neurodegenerations
Retrograde transport carries injury signals to the soma

stem: An investigator creates a sodium channel mutant in a neuron that inactivates faster after opening, with unchanged activation and recovery.
oneliner: Experiment: Na channel mutant that inactivates faster, activation and recovery unchanged → effect on action potential?
ask: Compared with the normal neuron, what is the most likely effect on the action potential?

whyNot.A: Recovery is **unchanged**, so the refractory period does not lengthen
whyNot.B: Less Na+ current slows rather than speeds conduction
whyNot.D: Rate depends on Na+ current, which here is **reduced**

why: If channels inactivate sooner, **less Na+ enters** before they close, so the peak is **lower**. Faster inactivation also hastens repolarisation.
chain: Less Na+ enters during the upstroke

idea.rule: Peak of the action potential reflects how much Na+ enters before inactivation.
also: Phenytoin and carbamazepine prolong Na channel inactivation (use-dependence)
Lidocaine blocks Na channels
Hyperkalemia inactivates Na channels
Tetrodotoxin blocks them entirely

stem: A squid axon is stimulated and recorded with a microelectrode. After the peak near +25 mV, the potential falls to about -100 mV, below the resting potential of -90 mV, before slowly returning.
oneliner: Experiment: axon AP falls from +25 to -100 mV, undershooting resting -90 mV → which ion permeability explains it?
ask: Increased permeability to which ion best explains the undershoot?

whyNot.A: Raising Na+ permeability would **depolarise**, not hyperpolarise
whyNot.C: Its equilibrium is near **resting potential**, so it cannot give a -100 mV undershoot
whyNot.E: Not a significant **membrane permeability** in the axon

why: Delayed **voltage-gated K+ channels** open as Na+ channels inactivate, driving the membrane toward **E_K (about -90 to -100 mV)**. Slow K+ channel closing gives the **after-hyperpolarisation**.
chain: Na+ channels inactivate at the peak

idea.rule: Repolarisation and undershoot are driven by raised K+ conductance.
also: Delayed rectifier K+ channels repolarise the cardiac action potential
Calcium-activated K+ channels in after-hyperpolarisation
Potassium channel blockers prolong the action potential (class III antiarrhythmics)
Resting potential is set mainly by K+ leak

stem: A 28-year-old man is startled by a car swerving at him and has a surge in plasma epinephrine within seconds.
oneliner: 28M + startled by swerving car + epinephrine surge → which transmitter acts directly on adrenal medulla?

whyNot.B: Released by **postganglionic** sympathetic fibres, not those to the medulla
whyNot.C: The adrenal **product**, not the signal to it
whyNot.D: A **central** excitatory transmitter, not used by autonomic preganglionic fibres
whyNot.E: A **central** neurotransmitter and kidney vasodilator, not the signal

why: Chromaffin cells are **modified postganglionic neurons** innervated directly by **preganglionic sympathetic** fibres. These release **ACh** onto **nicotinic receptors**, triggering catecholamine exocytosis.

idea.rule: All preganglionic autonomic fibres use acetylcholine.
also: Ganglionic transmission is nicotinic (Nn)
Sweat glands: sympathetic cholinergic postganglionic
Preganglionic parasympathetic: ACh
Hexamethonium blocks ganglia

stem: In an experiment, an action potential reaches a presynaptic terminal, and neurotransmitter release is measured.
oneliner: Experiment: action potential reaches presynaptic terminal → which channel must open for vesicle release?
ask: Which channel must open at the terminal for vesicles to fuse?

whyNot.A: Carries the **action potential** to the terminal but does not trigger fusion

why: Depolarisation opens **presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels**. Ca2+ binds **synaptotagmin** and drives **SNARE-mediated fusion** of vesicles.

idea.rule: Neurotransmitter release is triggered by presynaptic Ca2+ entry.
also: Lambert-Eaton: antibodies to presynaptic P/Q Ca2+ channels
Aminoglycosides reduce presynaptic Ca2+ entry at the neuromuscular junction
Magnesium blocks release
Omega-conotoxin blocks N-type Ca2+ channels

stem: At autopsy of a 62-year-old woman with a long-standing cerebellar ataxia syndrome, about 80% of Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex are lost.
oneliner: 62F + long-standing cerebellar ataxia + autopsy 80% Purkinje cell loss → which structure's neurons lose inhibition?

whyNot.B: Not a **Purkinje cell target**; receives cortical and nigral input
whyNot.C: Part of the **limbic** system, no Purkinje input
whyNot.E: A **cholinergic** system, not targeted by Purkinje cells

why: **Purkinje cells** are **GABAergic** and are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, **inhibiting the deep cerebellar nuclei**. Their loss disinhibits the **dentate**.

idea.rule: Purkinje cells are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex and are inhibitory, so losing them disinhibits the deep nuclei.
also: Chronic phenytoin toxicity causes Purkinje cell loss
Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration
Spinocerebellar ataxias
Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration

stem: A 68-year-old man died 8 weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct, from an unrelated cause. At autopsy the infarct is a small cavity whose rim has been filled in by proliferating cells with long branching processes; no fibrous scar is present.
oneliner: 68M + MCA infarct 8 wk earlier + cavity rimmed by proliferating branched cells, no fibrous scar -> which cell repaired it?
ask: Proliferation of which cell type repaired the damage?

whyNot.A: Clear **debris** but do not form the scar
whyNot.B: Make scars in **other tissues**, but CNS repair is glial
whyNot.E: Myelinate **peripheral** nerves, absent from the CNS

why: After CNS injury, **astrocytes proliferate** and form a **glial scar** (gliosis); **microglia clear necrotic debris**. This is the CNS equivalent of fibrous scarring.

idea.rule: CNS injury heals by astrocytic gliosis, not fibroblast scar.
also: Gliosis walling off a resolving traumatic contusion
Liquefactive necrosis then cavity
Multiple sclerosis plaques undergo gliosis
Peripheral nerve repair uses Schwann cells

stem: A 52-year-old woman has burning discomfort in both feet and noticed they look pink and feel hot and dry. Strength, reflexes and vibration sense are normal.
oneliner: 52F + burning feet + pink, hot, dry skin + normal strength, reflexes, vibration → which fibres are lost?
ask: Loss of which fibres best explains the skin changes?

whyNot.A: Carry **visceral sensation**; their loss does not affect sweat or vessel tone
whyNot.B: Do not supply **limb skin vessels or sweat glands**
whyNot.C: Loss gives **numbness**; normal vibration sense argues against
whyNot.E: Loss causes **weakness and atrophy**, which are absent

why: Loss of **sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone** causes **vasodilation (warm, pink)**, and loss of **cholinergic sudomotor** fibres stops sweating, giving **dry** skin.

idea.rule: Sympathetic denervation of skin gives warm, dry, vasodilated skin.
also: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Small fibre neuropathy
Horner syndrome (face)
Amyloid neuropathy

stem: A healthy 3-month-old boy is examined at a well-child visit. Stroking the lateral sole produces upgoing great toes on both feet. The rest of the examination is normal, and he is feeding and moving normally.
oneliner: 3-month-old boy + healthy + bilateral upgoing toes on sole stroking + normal exam → why?
ask: Which explanation best accounts for this response?

options.A: Axons have not reached the foot muscles
options.B: Corticospinal tracts are not yet myelinated
options.C: Monosynaptic reflexes are not yet established
options.E: Cerebral cortex injury from birth hypoxia

whyNot.A: Foot movements are present, so the **muscles are innervated**
whyNot.D: Muscle immaturity would not give an **extensor** response
whyNot.E: He is **otherwise normal**; injury would show deficits

why: The **corticospinal tracts myelinate over the first 1-2 years**. Until then, the **primitive extensor plantar reflex persists**; myelination restores descending inhibition.
chain: Corticospinal tracts myelinate during the first 1-2 years
Without descending control the primitive reflex persists
Great toe extends on sole stroking

idea.rule: Primitive reflexes are normal in infancy and fade as descending corticospinal control myelinates.
also: Adult Babinski means upper motor neuron lesion
Primitive reflexes disappear as the cortex matures
Moro and rooting reflexes fade in months
Persistent primitive reflexes suggest cerebral palsy
